newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Confident Australian dlr strikes relaxed pose.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Confident Australian dlr strikes relaxed pose.

text.p: The Australian dollar struck a relaxed pose Thursday as a U.S. holiday offered further reason to stick to the week's well defined range around 81 cents.

Option-related offers at US$0.8130 were impeding the uptrend but chart signs were glowing green for a long term rally to 84 cents, and Japanese demand for yen/A$ samurais looked safe now that a subdued economy had put paid to tightening fears there.

Data showing a slowing in domestic wages growth stirred the dust which had begun to gather on rate talk here, but not by enough for analysts to change their view that a cut was at best an evens chance and then not until February or March.
By 4.45 pm (0545 GMT) the dollar was getting into the holiday spirit at US$0.8093/98 having hardly shifted from its early US$0.8103/08 and Wednesday's late US$0.8095/00.
But this sleepy performance was considered impressive, all the same, since the currency had resisted all efforts to force a substantial correction of last week's 2-1/2 cent surge.

It was also holding close to a four year peak on the yen at 91.60/70 from 91.56/66 Wednesday and near a five year high on its trade weighted index at 59.8. And dealers looked for further gains since the flow of funds from Japan seemed assured after Wednesday's subdued Tankan survey quashed talk of a BOJ hike.
The closely watched business survey suggested Japan's recovery was gradual at best and sent yields on the 10-year JGB diving 15 basis points to 2.415 percent.
That widened the Australian dollar's yield advantage -- a comparable bond here pays 7.11 percent -- and suggested it would not be narrowing much soon, at least from the Japanese side.
There was still a risk rates could come down here, however, given sluggish employment and improving inflationary conditions.
Evidence of both was provided today with skilled vacancies falling 0.7 percent, the 11th consecutive monthly drop, and enterprise wages growth slowing.
The latter was important as the Reserve Bank had highlighted enterprise deals as a leading indicator of wage trends in its last quarterly report on the economy.

The Department of Industrial Relations said annualised wages based on agreements covering almost 200,000 employees rose 4.8 percent in the September quarter, down from a revised 5.3 percent in Q2 -- it was originally reported at 5.6 percent.
Private sector wages rose an average of 5.3 percent in Q3, down from a revised 6.1 percent -- originally 6.6 percent.
Analysts reckoned the slowing might make the RBA a little more comfortable about cutting rates.
But some noted the private sector was still running above the RBA's comfort level of 5.0 percent.

"With underlying inflation likely to remain in the RBA's 2-3 percent target zone over 1997, there is probably scope for one more interest rate cut," said Andrew Pease, chief economist at Nomura Research Australia.

Since the last reduction on November 6 had hardly had time to make itself felt, he doubted the bank would countenance a move at its December board meeting next week but thought it might reconsider in February or March after Q4 inflation and wages data were known.
"But with wages concerns persisting and the economy strengthening in 1997, sentiment is likely to turn towards judging the timing of next rate rise from mid-1997," he said.
RBA governor Ian Macfarlane may shed some light on the bank's current thinking in a speech to a business dinner tonight entitled "The Task for Monetary Policy".

The next data release of note is balance of payments for October on Friday. The current account deficit is expected to remain around a tolerable A$1.6 billion after widening to A$1.69 billion in September.
